source_text: Igitur cum cognoscendo deo hominem prospexisset bonitas dei ipsius, etiam hoc praeconio suo addidit, quod prius domicilium homini commentata est aliquam [postmodum] molem maximam, postmodum et maiorem, ut in magna tamquam in minore proluderet atque proficeret et ita de bono dei, id est de magno, ad optimum quoque eius, id est ad maius habitaculum, promoueretur. adhibet operi bono optimum etiam ministrum, sermonem suum: eructauit, inquit, cor meum sermonem optimum. agnoscat hinc primum fructum optimum, utique optimae arboris, Marcion. imperitissimus rusticus quidem malam in bonam inseruit. sed non ualebit blasphemiae surculus; arescet cum suo artifice et ita se bonae arboris natura testabitur. aspice ad summam, qualia sermo fructificauerit: et dixit deus: fiat, et factum est, et uidit deus quia bonum, non quasi nesciens bonum nisi uideret, sed quia bonum, ideo uidens, honorans et consignans et dispungens bonitatem operum dignatione conspectus. sic et benedicebat quae benefaciebat, ut tibi totus deus commendaretur, bonus et dicere et facere. male dicere adhuc sermo non norat, quia nec malefacere. uidebimus causas, quae hoc quoque a deo exegerunt. interim mundus ex bonis omnibus constitit, satis praemonstrans, quantum boni pararetur illi, cui praeparabatur hoc totum. quis denique dignus incolere dei opera quam ipsius imago et similitudo? eam quoque bonitas et quidem operantior operata est, non imperiali uerbo, sed familiari manu, etiam uerbo blandiente praemisso: faciamus hominem ad imaginem et similitudinem nostram. bonitas dixit; bonitas finxit de limo in tantam substantiam carnis, ex una materia tot qualitatibus exstructam; bonitas inflauit in animam, non mortuam, sed uiuam; bonitas praefecit uniuersis fruendis atque regnandis, etiam cognomiuandis; bonitas amplius delicias adiecit homini, ut, quamquam totius orbis . possidens, in amoenioribus moraretur, translatus in paradisum — iam tunc de mundo in ecclesiam —; eadem bonitas et adiutorium prospexit, ne quid non boni. non est enim, inquit, bonum solum esse hominem. sciebat illi sexum Mariae et deinceps ecclesiae profuturum. sed et quam arguis legem, quam in controuersias torques, bonitas irrogauit, consulens homini, quo deo adhaereret, ne non tam liber quam abiectus uideretur, aequandus famulis suis, ceteris animalibus, solutis a deo et ex fastidio liberis, sed ut solus homo gloriaretur, quod solus dignus fuisset, qui legem a deo sumeret, utque animal rationale, intellectus et scientiae capax, ipsa quoque libertate rationali contineretur, ei subiectus, qui subiecerat illi omnia. cuius legis obseruandae consilium bonitas pariter adscripsit: qua die autem ederitis, morte moriemini. benignissime enim demonstrauit exitum transgressionis, ne ignorantia periculi neglegentiam iuuaret obsequii. porro si legis imponendae ratio praecessit, sequebatur etiam obseruandae, ut poena transgressioni adscriberetur, quam tamen euenire noluit qui ante praedixit. I agnosce igitur bonitatem dei nostri interim uel bucusque ex operibus bonis, ex benedictionibus bonis, ex indulgentiis, ex prouidentiis, ex legibus et praemonitionibus bonis et benignis.\'
pass_a_gloss: Therefore when the goodness of God had looked out for man by knowing him, it also added this to its proclamation, that previously it had prepared a certain dwelling for man, afterwards a very great one, and afterwards an even greater one, so that in a great one as if in a smaller one it might bring forth and profit, and thus from the goodness of God, that is from the great one, it might be promoted to the best one, that is to the greater dwelling. It applies to the good work the best minister also, its word: my heart, it says, has uttered the best word. Let Marcion recognize from here the first best fruit, certainly of the best tree. The most inexperienced rustic indeed grafts a bad one into a good one. But the sprout of blasphemy will not prevail; it will wither away with its craftsman, and thus the nature of the good tree will prove itself. Look to the sum, of what kind the word has brought forth fruit: and God said, let it be, and it was made, and God saw that it was good, not as if not knowing it was good unless he saw, but because it was good, therefore seeing, honoring and sealing and bestowing the goodness of the works with the dignity of the gaze. Thus it also blessed what it benefited, so that all of God might be commended to you, good in both speaking and doing. The word did not yet know how to speak evil, because neither did it know how to do evil. We will see the causes which also demanded this from God. Meanwhile the world consists of all good things, sufficiently demonstrating how much good was being prepared for the one for whom all this was being prepared. Who finally is worthy to inhabit the works of God except the image and likeness of God himself? This also the goodness, and indeed the more operative one, has made, not with an imperial word, but with a familiar hand, and also with a word that flatters, having been sent ahead: let us make man in our image and likeness. Goodness spoke; goodness formed from clay into such a great substance of flesh, constructed from one material with so many qualities; goodness breathed into the soul, not a dead one, but a living one; goodness put in charge of all things to be enjoyed and ruled, and also to be named; goodness added delights to man, so that, although possessing the whole world, he might linger in more pleasant places, having been transferred into paradise — already then from the world into the church —; the same goodness also looked out for help, lest there be anything not good. For it is not good, it says, for man to be alone. It knew that sex would be profitable for him, and thereafter for the church. But also the law which you accuse, which you twist into controversies, goodness imposed, consulting for man, so that he might adhere to God, lest he seem not so much free as cast off, equal to his servants, the other animals, released by God and freed from disgust, but so that man alone might glory, because he alone was worthy, who might take the law from God, and so that as a rational animal, capable of intellect and knowledge, he might also be contained by rational freedom, being subject to the one who had subjected all things to him. The plan of observing this law goodness equally prescribed: on the day when you eat, you will die by death. For it most kindly demonstrated the outcome of transgression, lest ignorance of the danger might assist negligence of obedience. Furthermore, if the reason for imposing the law preceded, the observance of it also followed, so that punishment might be ascribed to transgression, which however he who had previously foretold did not want to happen. Therefore recognize the goodness of our God meanwhile or up to this point from the good works, from the good blessings, from the indulgences, from the providences, from the good and kind laws and warnings.

choices.why: to maintain consistency in referring to God's attributes

bible_refs.note: non est enim bonum solum esse hominem

pass_b_english: Once God's goodness looked out for humanity by knowing it, the goodness added a further claim to its own proclamation: it had first prepared a dwelling for human beings, then a very great one, and finally an even greater one. The purpose was that a person might first exercise and grow in a great dwelling as if it were a smaller one, and so advance from God's goodness — that is, the great — to the highest expression of that goodness — that is, the greater dwelling. The goodness also appointed the best possible minister for its good work: its own Word. 'My heart has uttered the best word,' it says. Let Marcion recognize from this the first, best fruit — certainly of the best tree. The most ignorant peasant grafts a bad shoot onto a good one, but the shoot of blasphemy will not prevail; it will wither along with its craftsman, and in that way the nature of the good tree will prove itself. Look at the sum of things and see what kind of fruit the Word has produced: God said, 'Let it be,' and it came to be, and God saw that it was good — not as though he did not know it was good unless he saw it, but because it was good he saw it, honoring and sealing and bestowing the goodness of the works with the dignity of his gaze (Genesis 1:3; Genesis 1:31). Thus he also blessed what he had benefited, so that all of God might be commended to you as good in both speaking and doing. The Word did not yet know how to speak evil, because it did not know how to do evil. We will see the causes that demanded this from God as well. Meanwhile the world consists entirely of good things, sufficiently demonstrating how much good was being prepared for the one for whom all this was being prepared. Who, finally, is worthy to inhabit God's works except God's own image and likeness? That image, too, goodness — and indeed the more operative goodness — brought about, not with an imperial decree but with a familiar hand, preceded by a coaxing word: 'Let us make humanity in our image and likeness.' Goodness spoke; goodness formed clay into so great a substance of flesh, constructed from a single material with so many qualities; goodness breathed into the soul — not a dead one, but a living one; goodness placed humanity in charge of all things to be enjoyed and ruled, and also to be named; goodness added further delights so that, although possessing the whole world, humanity might linger in more pleasant places, transferred into paradise — already then from the world into the church; the same goodness also looked out for help, lest anything not good remain. 'It is not good for the human to be alone,' it says (Genesis 2:18). God knew that sex would be profitable for the man, and thereafter for the church. But the law that you accuse, that you twist into controversies — goodness imposed that, too, consulting for the human's sake, so that he might cling to God, lest he seem not so much free as cast off, equal to his servants, the other animals, released by God and freed from disgust. Rather, goodness intended that the human alone might glory, because he alone was worthy to receive the law from God, and that as a rational creature capable of intellect and knowledge, he might also be contained by rational freedom, subject to the one who had subjected all things to him. Goodness equally prescribed the plan for observing this law: 'On the day you eat of it, you will die by death' (Genesis 2:17). For it most kindly demonstrated the outcome of transgression, lest ignorance of the danger assist negligence in obedience. Furthermore, if the reason for imposing the law came first, the observance of it followed as well, so that punishment might be ascribed to transgression — which, however, the one who had foretold it beforehand did not want to happen. Therefore recognize the goodness of our God, at least up to this point, from the good works, from the good blessings, from the indulgences, from the providences, from the good and kind laws and warnings.

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the Latin text. Pass A provides a faithful literal rendering, and Pass B provides a fluent rendering that correctly incorporates the required scripture citations (Genesis 1:3, 1:31, 2:18, 2:17) corresponding to the Latin clauses. All nuances regarding the agency of 'bonitas' and the distinctions between the 'imperial' and 'familiar' modes of creation are preserved.

source: 'bonitas dixit; bonitas finxit de limo in tantam substantiam carnis, ex una materia tot qualitatibus exstructam'; English: 'goodness spoke; goodness formed from clay into such a great substance of flesh, constructed from one material with so many qualities'
